processing: A blend: tea, usually black, is mixed with flowers, dried fruit or spices, and commercial versions also get part of their taste from added flavourings.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; the base tea comes from any season, and blends mostly appear for the winter holidays.
appearance_dry: Dark leaf flecked with pieces of spice, peel or flowers, varying by blender.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish brown, as with most black tea blends.
appearance_wet: Dark leaf mixed with softened bits of fruit and spice.
taste_profile: Varies by recipe; usually warm spice and dried fruit over a plain black tea base.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style. Follow the blender's advice, since recipes differ, and shorten the steep if it turns bitter.

vintage_note: Sold seasonally as a holiday blend, not by harvest year, and most shops stock it around the end of the year. Flavoured blends lose aroma with time, so buy the current season's batch and drink it within the winter or soon after.
description:
Christmas tea, or thé de Noël, is not a single recipe but a kind of seasonal blend: usually black tea with festive spices, fruit and peel. Many tea houses and brands sell their own.

The base is mostly there to carry the additions. Cinnamon, orange peel, apple, almond and vanilla are common, and French usage counts these blends among flavoured teas since commercial versions usually get part of their taste from added aroma.

Expect spice and sweet orange first, with mild black tea behind. Use Western-style steeps and stop at about four minutes, because the spices stay pleasant but the tea can go bitter.

Read the ingredients when you buy. The word Christmas tells you nothing about the recipe, and the differences between real pieces and flavouring are large. Freshness matters more than origin here.

A good mug of it goes well with gingerbread or anything with dried fruit.
history: No single origin is documented for Christmas tea as a general idea. French usage counts thé de Noël among flavoured teas, and tea sellers elsewhere also offer blends under the name. The term covers a seasonal shelf more than any fixed tea.
